name: Groin Adductor Slide
execution: Stand on a smooth floor in socks, or use a slide board. Place one foot on a slider or towel. Start with feet together. Slowly slide the foot outward — controlled by the adductor of that leg. Go as wide as comfortable, feeling the groin stretch under load. Pull the foot back in using the adductor — the concentric return. Complete 8-10 reps each side. Control every centimetre of the slide.
why: The groin adductor slide eccentrically loads the adductors through the exact skating stride range — it is the most direct off-ice translation of the groin's role in controlling the stride width and generating medial force. Regular eccentric adductor work has been shown to increase adductor tendon cross-sectional area, making the tendon more resistant to the repetitive strain that causes chronic groin problems in skaters.
transfer: Active groin mobility — replaces the passive stretch with dynamic control. Pair with Copenhagen plank for full adductor coverage: stretch + strength = injury-proof groin.
cues: "Wide stance" · "Shift weight to one side" · "Lower into a side lunge" · "Slide foot out"
mistakes: Sliding too fast — the entire value is in the slow, resisted control. Going beyond comfortable range before you have the strength — build range gradually over weeks. Only sliding one direction — equally important to train the non-dominant side. Skipping it because it feels fine — groin injuries don't announce themselves before they happen.
progression: Progress: Lateral lunge to slider — combines bodyweight load with the adductor slide demand. | Regress: Seated butterfly with gentle knee press — passive adductor stretch to begin restoring range.

name: Inchworm Walk
execution: Stand tall, feet hip-width apart. Hinge forward at the hips — KEEP LEGS AS STRAIGHT AS POSSIBLE — and place hands on the floor. Walk the hands forward until you're in a high plank position. Hold the plank 1-2 seconds — chest stable, hips level, core tight. Walk the feet UP to the hands in small steps — legs stay as straight as the hamstrings allow. Stand up. That's one rep. 5-10 reps.
why: The inchworm walk combines three full-body qualities in one move: posterior-chain mobility (hamstring stretch when walking feet to hands), core control + shoulder stability (the plank position), and full-body coordination. For hockey players whose hamstrings are chronically tight from the skating stride, this is one of the few warm-up movements that simultaneously LOADS the hamstrings while stretching them — mobility through strength. It's the single best general warm-up before a leg-day session.
transfer: Full-body mobility + core control + shoulder stability in one move. Loosens tight hamstrings (the #1 hockey limitation) while building the plank position used in skating mechanics. Daily warm-up forever. Three minutes of inchworms beats 10 minutes of static stretching.
cues: "Stand tall. Hinge forward" · "Walk hands out on the floor until you're in a high plank. Hold 1 second. Walk feet UP to your hands (keep legs as straight as possible). Stand up. Repeat."
mistakes: Bending the knees on the walk-in — defeats the hamstring stretch. Keep legs as straight as your mobility allows. Letting hips sag in the plank — wasted core opportunity. Brace it. Rushing the walks — slow and controlled, especially on the feet-walk-in phase. Skipping the plank pause — that's where the shoulder and core stability lives.
progression: Progress: Inchworm + push-up — add 1 push-up at the plank phase. Doubles as upper-body activation. | Regress: Short inchworm (walk hands out only halfway, not all the way to plank) — same pattern, less ROM demand.

name: Barbell Back Squat
execution: Set the bar at upper-back height in a power rack. Step under, bar across upper traps (high bar) or rear delts (low bar). Brace abs HARD, take a tight grip outside shoulders. Step back 2-3 paces with feet shoulder-width, toes slightly out. Initiate the descent by sitting hips back AND breaking at knees simultaneously. Descend until hip crease is below knee — 'parallel'. Knees track over toes. Drive back up by pushing the floor away — chest stays up, no forward dump. Lock out fully at top with hips and knees extended.
why: The back squat is the single most-studied lower-body strength builder. For hockey, it develops the quad/glute/hamstring chain that produces every skating stride. Athletes with a back squat ≥ 1.6× bodyweight outperform weaker athletes in skating speed by 12-15%. The depth and load capacity also build the connective tissue resilience required for in-season durability.
transfer: Foundation of lower body strength — drives skating power. Three reps at 85%, four sets, three minutes rest. The hockey-specific max strength prescription. No shortcuts.
cues: "Chest up" · "Knees track toes" · "Break parallel" · "Drive through heels"
mistakes: Knees collapsing inward (valgus) — major injury risk. Cue 'spread the floor'. Heels coming up — usually ankle mobility issue. Use 5-10mm lifters or work ankle mobility. Forward dump (chest collapses) — usually weak upper back. Slow the eccentric, fix by adding rows. Cutting depth — limits glute/hamstring recruitment. Better to drop the weight and squat full range.
progression: Progress: Pause squat (3-second pause at depth) once form is dialed. Builds bottom-position strength for skating starts. | Regress: Goblet squat with kettlebell. Easier to keep upright posture, builds the pattern with less spinal load.

name: Calf Raise Iso Hold
execution: Stand with the balls of your feet on the edge of a step (or on flat floor). Push to the very top of a calf raise — heels as high as they go. HOLD. Weight stays on the balls of the feet, ankles fully extended, knees soft. Single-leg version: same setup, one foot only (other foot lifted off). Hold steady — no bouncing or dropping mid-hold. Lower under control. Repeat or switch.
why: Ankle stiffness — the foot's ability to act like a spring rather than a soft pad on push-off — is one of the most under-trained qualities in hockey training, and it's directly tied to skating speed. Each stride, the foot transfers energy from leg drive into ice push, and that transfer is lossy if the ankle is sloppy. Holding the top of a calf raise builds soleus and gastrocnemius isometric strength — the muscles that lock the ankle into rigid spring mode. The bonus: same muscles that protect against Achilles strains and shin-splint pain. Cheap to do, high carryover, almost no one trains it. Easy win.
transfer: Ankle stiffness is the most under-trained quality in skating — it determines how much of your leg drive actually transfers into ice push. Iso-holding the top of a calf raise builds it directly. Drop to single-leg as soon as two-foot is easy — same muscle, way more load.
cues: "Stand on the edge of a step (or flat floor). Push to the very top of a calf raise — heels as high as they go. HOLD. Two-foot for beginner" · "Single-leg for advanced."
mistakes: Rocking outward onto the pinky-toe edge of the foot — keep weight on the big toe through to the second-toe ball. Bending the knees to cheat the top — knees stay soft but extended. Bouncing in and out of the hold — defeats the iso; one continuous push to the top. Going single-leg before bilateral is bombproof — earn 45-60s solid two-foot first.
progression: Progress: Single-leg calf raise iso hold. Or weighted (dumbbell in hand, kettlebell racked). | Regress: Bilateral on flat floor (no step edge) — shorter range, same iso quality.

name: Front Squat
execution: Set the bar in the front rack position — resting on the front deltoids, elbows HIGH and forward. Feet shoulder-width, toes slightly out. Keep elbows high throughout — if they drop the bar rolls forward. Sit DOWN between the knees — more vertical torso than a back squat. Descend until hip crease is below the knee. Knees track over toes. Drive the floor away to stand — chest up, elbows stay high.
why: The front squat demands a more upright torso than the back squat, which better replicates the skating position — knees forward, hips loaded, spine tall. It develops quad dominance while requiring serious upper-back and core strength to hold the bar. For hockey players it is an excellent tool for building knee strength and the forward-lean positioning used in the skating crouch.
transfer: Builds quad strength and upright posture — mimics skating stance. Goalies live in this position. If you play goalie, front squat is non-negotiable.
cues: "Elbows high" · "Keep bar on front delts" · "Stay upright" · "Deep squat"
mistakes: Elbows dropping — kills the front rack and dumps the bar forward. Elbows up, always. Heels coming up — ankle mobility issue. Work dorsiflexion or use small heel lift temporarily. Leaning forward — front squat requires more upright torso than back squat. If you lean, the load is too heavy. Wrist pain in the rack position — work wrist flexibility or use a cross-arm grip temporarily.
progression: Progress: Pause front squat (3s at the bottom) — builds bottom-position strength for low skating stance. | Regress: Goblet squat — same upright torso demand with much easier load management.

name: Hang Power Clean
execution: Start with the bar hanging at hip/thigh level — knees slightly bent, hips back. This is the 'hang' position: flat back, bar touching thighs, weight on mid-foot. Initiate by driving the hips FORWARD explosively — the hip snap drives the bar upward. As the bar rises, shrug the traps aggressively, then pull the elbows HIGH and outside. Drop under the bar quickly — rotating elbows forward to catch in the front rack. Catch with knees slightly bent. Stand tall. Lower the bar to hang. Repeat.
why: The hang power clean is the most complete athletic power exercise — it trains triple extension (ankle, knee, hip) at maximum velocity plus the rapid descent under the bar (catching phase), which builds the reactive strength pattern of absorbing and redirecting force on the ice. Many NHL teams use the power clean as their primary power development tool precisely because it trains the entire kinetic chain simultaneously.
transfer: Trains explosive triple extension (ankle/knee/hip) under load — the exact pattern of a skating stride. Builds rate of force development. Requires coaching — if you have not been taught the catch position, substitute trap-bar jump or hang clean PULL (no-catch variant). Triphasic Phase 2 (max power). The bridge between heavy strength and plyometrics. Best of both worlds.
cues: "Bar at hip" · "Hinge to mid-thigh" · "Explode hips through" · "Shrug hard" · "Catch in quarter squat. Speed > weight. If the catch is shaky" · "Stop — drop to a clean pull (no catch) until coached."
mistakes: Pulling with the arms too early — the arms just guide the bar. Power comes from the hip drive. Bar drifting away from the body — keep it close throughout the pull. Catching with a stiff lower body — the catch requires a quarter squat to absorb. Ego loading — technique falls apart above a certain weight. Keep it clean.
progression: Progress: Full power clean from the floor — adds a more challenging starting position. | Regress: Kettlebell swing — same hip drive mechanics without the catch complexity.

name: Hip Airplane Hold
execution: Stand on one leg. Standing knee can be slightly soft (not locked, not bent). Hinge at the hip — torso drops forward, back leg lifts behind you. Continue until torso and back leg form a straight line parallel to the floor (a 'T' from the side). Arms extend out wide to the sides for balance. Square the hips — point both hip bones at the floor (don't let the back-leg hip rotate open). HOLD. Standing leg solid, no twisting. Stand under control. Switch.
why: The hip airplane is the deep-stabilizer test most off-ice training programs miss. Holding a single-leg T-position — torso and back leg parallel to the floor, hips square — recruits the glute medius, deep hip rotators, and posterior-chain stabilizers that control hip rotation under load. For hockey, that's the EXACT muscle system that keeps a skate edge tracking through a tight turn: when an athlete's outside hip rotates uncontrolled, they lose the edge. Adding 15-25s isometric holds in this position builds the rotational stability that pays off in cleaner turns, better balance through contact, and dramatically lower rates of nagging hip and groin issues across a season.
transfer: Single-leg balance plus hip-rotation control under hold — the same deep stabilizer system that keeps a skate edge tracking through tight turns. Most overlooked iso in hockey training. Catching yourself with the back leg means the hold is lost. End the set there — quality over time.
cues: "Single-leg stance. Hinge at the hip — torso and back leg form a straight "T" parallel to the floor. Arms out wide. HOLD without letting the hip drop or rotate. Switch legs."
mistakes: Back-leg hip rotating open (turning sideways) — kills the whole point; force both hip bones to point down. Standing knee locking out fully — keep it soft so the hip muscles work, not the joint. Catching with the back foot when balance fails — once that happens, end the set; the hold is over. Arching the lower back — torso stays straight, like a board parallel to the floor.
progression: Progress: Eyes closed (removes visual balance feedback — makes it ~30% harder). Or hold a light dumbbell in the lifted arm. | Regress: Hand on a wall or pole for balance — same T position, less stability demand.
muscles: Glute medius, Hip stabilizers, Hamstrings, Core

name: Leg Extension (Machine)
execution: Sit on the leg extension machine. Pad sits just above the ankles. Grip the handles for stability. Back flat against the pad. Extend both legs smoothly to full lockout — quads fully contracted. Pause 1-2 seconds at full extension — this is where VMO fires hardest. Lower slowly — 3 seconds — back to the start position. Do not swing the torso to help the lift.',.
why: The leg extension isolates the quadriceps in open-chain knee extension — building the VMO (inner quad) strength that stabilises the patella tracking and prevents 'runner's knee', which is common in hockey players from heavy skating volume. While not a sport-specific movement, it is an important accessory exercise for correcting quad development gaps and supporting knee joint health.
transfer: Isolates quads — builds terminal knee extension strength for skating. Don't do leg extensions on heavy squat day. Pick one heavy quad stimulus per session — they don't add, they redundancy.
cues: "Full range of motion" · "Squeeze at top" · "Slow lowering"
mistakes: Partial range — full extension is required for VMO activation. Fast lowering — the slow eccentric builds the patella-stabilising strength. Too heavy — should be able to do full range with smooth control.',. Using this as a substitute for squats — it supplements, never replaces, compound work.',.
progression: Progress: Single-leg extension — identifies and corrects left-right quad imbalances. | Regress: Terminal knee extension (TKE) with band — lighter, safer, great VMO activation.',

name: Leg Press
execution: Sit in the leg press. Feet shoulder-width on the platform, mid-height. Unrack the weight. Lower the platform by bending the knees. Descend until knees reach 90° — thighs parallel to the platform. Drive through the full foot — not just the toes — to press back to start. Do NOT lock the knees out explosively — stop just short of full lock.',. Keep the lower back flat against the pad throughout.',.
why: The leg press allows higher absolute loads than the squat with significantly less spinal compression — making it ideal for developing pure quad and glute strength in players with lower-back limitations or during high-volume phases when spinal fatigue is a concern. Sled-press force output correlates well with skating acceleration, and the machine's guided path allows full attention on maximal force production.
transfer: Safe way to load leg strength without spinal compression. Leg press is supplemental, not primary. Heavy squats remain king. Use leg press to add volume without CNS cost.
cues: "Feet shoulder-width" · "Lower to 90°" · "Press through heels" · "Do not lock knees"
mistakes: Feet too low — increases knee stress. Mid-platform is neutral.',. Lower back peeling off the seat at the bottom — reduce the range of motion.',. Locking out the knees with a jolt — controlled extension only.',. Using the leg press as a squat replacement entirely — it doesn't train stabilisers.',.
progression: Progress: Single-leg press — unilateral loading corrects imbalances and increases demand.', | Regress: Bodyweight squat — learn the pattern before adding any external load.',

name: Pause Squat
execution: Set up exactly as a back squat — bar on upper back, feet shoulder-width. Descend under full control to the bottom position (hip crease below knee). STOP completely — eliminate all bounce. Pause for 3 full seconds. During the pause: stay braced, knees out, chest up. Do not relax. Drive back to the top — this is harder than any regular squat. Breathe at the top between reps. Don't rush.
why: The pause squat (3-5 second hold at the bottom) eliminates the stretch-reflex bounce that most athletes rely on, forcing the muscles to produce force from a dead stop — identical to the demand of a skating start from a stationary position. It builds the bottom-position quad and glute strength that is significantly undertrained in normal squatting and directly improves first-step quickness from a standstill.
transfer: Eliminates the bounce — trains true strength from a dead stop. Three reps × four sets at 70%. Pause squats teach patience. Pause squats also expose every weakness in the bottom position.
cues: "Squat to parallel" · "Pause 3 seconds" · "No bounce" · "Drive explosively up"
mistakes: Bouncing even slightly out of the hole — any bounce defeats the purpose. Relaxing the core during the pause — stay fully braced throughout. Too heavy — pause squats require 10-20% less load than regular squats. Short pause — 3 seconds minimum. Count it out loud if needed.
progression: Progress: Tempo squat (5s down, 3s pause, explosive up) — adds eccentric control to the pause. | Regress: Goblet squat with pause — lighter load, easier to maintain upright torso.

name: Spanish Squat (Isometric)
execution: Anchor a heavy resistance band around a sturdy upright at knee height. Step inside the band so it wraps around the back of both knees. Walk backward until the band is taut and actively pulling you forward. Sit back into a quarter-to-half squat — torso tall and vertical (this is the giveaway: no forward lean). Knees stay tracking over the toes; resist the band's forward pull. HOLD. Hold until quads burn out. Step forward to release.
why: The Spanish squat is the gold-standard isometric for the patellar tendon — the structure that takes the brunt of every stop, every crossover acceleration, and every change of direction a skater performs. Anchoring a heavy band around the back of the knees creates a horizontal pulling force that has to be resisted by quad isometric contraction, loading the tendon directly without the spinal compression of a back squat. Sports-medicine clinics use this as the FIRST-line protocol for jumper's knee (patellar tendinopathy) — both for treatment and prevention. Hockey players who add 2 × 30-60s of Spanish squats per week experience dramatically lower rates of nagging anterior knee pain across a season.
transfer: The gold-standard patellar tendon isometric — bulletproofs the knees against the constant stop-start loading of skating. Sports medicine's primary protocol for jumper's-knee prevention and rehab. Make the band heavy enough that it actively pulls — if you're not resisting, the iso isn't there. Add band tension before adding time.
cues: "Heavy band anchored at knee-height around a sturdy post. Step inside so it wraps the back of both knees. Sit back into a quarter-to-half squat — band pulls forward" · "You resist. Torso tall. HOLD."
mistakes: Leaning forward at the hips — converts it into a regular squat and unloads the patellar tendon. Band too light — if you're not actively pulling against it, the iso stimulus isn't there. Use the heaviest band that lets you hold for ≥30s. Knees caving inward — push out against the band actively. Going too deep (full squat) — quarter-to-half is the working range; deeper makes it a leg workout, not a tendon iso.
progression: Progress: Heavier band + longer hold (60-90s). Or single-leg Spanish squat with band on one knee only. | Regress: Lighter band + shallower depth (quarter-squat only). Or bodyweight wall sit while you build base quad endurance.

name: Standing Calf Raise (DBs)
execution: Stand on the edge of a step or plate — heels hanging off the edge. Lower heels as far below the step as possible — full stretch at the bottom. Push up onto the balls of your feet as high as possible — full contraction at top. Pause 1 second at the top. Lower for 3 seconds. Keep knees straight for gastrocnemius; slightly bent for soleus. Use one leg at a time for maximum loading.
why: The calf (gastrocnemius + soleus) is the primary ankle plantar flexor — it provides the final snap in each skating stride and generates the spring energy through the Achilles tendon. Weak calves are a direct brake on stride frequency and power. They are also the first line of defense against Achilles tendinopathy, which is chronically undertrained in hockey players who rely entirely on skating for lower-leg development.
transfer: Builds calf strength for explosive push-off and skating acceleration. Add tempo: 3 seconds down, 1 second hold at top. Tempo work is where calves actually grow.
cues: "Full range of motion" · "Pause at top" · "Slow lower" · "Use full heel drop"
mistakes: Partial range — bounce-style reps with no stretch. Full range only. Both legs always — single-leg is where real strength lives. Skipping the slow eccentric — Achilles injury prevention requires eccentric loading. Treating calves as an afterthought — 3 sets twice a week is enough to make a real difference.
progression: Progress: Single-leg weighted calf raise (hold dumbbell) — dramatically increases load. | Regress: Double-leg calf raise with bodyweight — build the pattern before going single-leg.

name: Tempo Squat (3-1-1)
execution: Set up for a back squat — bar on upper back, feet shoulder-width. Lower over 3-5 seconds — count it out. Controlled, not grinding. Pause 2-3 seconds at the bottom — no bounce, stay tight. Drive back up as EXPLOSIVELY as possible — maximum intent on the concentric. The contrast between slow descent and explosive ascent is the stimulus. Rest fully between reps at the top.
why: The tempo squat (slow eccentric + pause + explosive concentric) develops all three components of the strength-speed curve simultaneously. The slow eccentric (3-5 seconds) builds quad and glute time-under-tension; the pause eliminates the stretch reflex; the explosive concentric trains rate of force development. For hockey players, this combination directly improves the first-step explosiveness that comes after absorbing a hockey stop.
transfer: Builds hypertrophy and connective tissue strength with time under tension. Three sets × 8 with controlled tempo. Goblet or front loading is ideal — back squat tempo is brutal on the spine.
cues: "3 seconds down" · "1 second pause" · "1 second up — controlled throughout"
mistakes: Relaxing at the bottom — stay fully braced during the pause. Explosive on the way down too — only the eccentric is slow. Not the concentric. Too heavy — tempo squats require 15-20% less load than regular squats. Rushing the eccentric — count it out loud if needed.
progression: Progress: Longer eccentric (5-6 seconds) or longer pause (4-5 seconds) as you adapt. | Regress: Goblet squat with 2s pause — same concept with a lighter, more forgiving implement.

name: Barbell Hip Thrust
execution: Sit on the floor with upper back against a sturdy bench, knees bent, feet flat. Roll a loaded barbell over your hips. Use a barbell pad — do NOT skip this. Drive feet through the floor, extend hips upward. Squeeze glutes HARD at the top. Ribs DOWN, chin tucked — don't hyperextend the lower back to fake range of motion. Pause 1-2 seconds at the top. This is where 80% of the glute work happens. Lower under control, don't crash the bar to the floor.
why: The barbell hip thrust isolates the glutes with the bar's resistance vector horizontal — exactly the direction of force production in skating push-off. It produces roughly 3× higher glute activation than back squats at equivalent loads. For hockey players, strong glutes mean better stride length and reduced knee/lower-back injury risk.
transfer: Directly trains glute extension — the primary muscle in skating push-off. Most hockey players are quad-dominant. Hip thrusts are how you flip that. Train the glutes, train the skating.
cues: "Upper back on bench" · "Bar on hips" · "Drive through heels" · "Squeeze glutes at top"
mistakes: Hyperextending the lower back to fake higher hips — defeats the exercise. Ribs DOWN. Feet too close — converts it to a quad exercise. Heels should be ~12-18 inches from glutes at top. Pushing through toes — should feel mid-foot/heel pressure for glute engagement. No pad on the bar — stops you from using meaningful loads. Get the pad.
progression: Progress: Single-leg hip thrust (foot elevated on bench) — highest hockey transfer due to unilateral loading. | Regress: Bodyweight glute bridge first. Learn the squeeze pattern before loading the bar.

name: Conventional Deadlift
execution: Stand with feet hip-width, bar over mid-foot (1 inch from shins). Hinge at the hips and grip the bar — double overhand or mixed grip. Set the back: chest tall, lats engaged, bar close to shins. Big breath into the belly, brace the core 360°. Push the floor away — leg drive first, then hips and back rise together. Bar stays in contact with the legs the entire way up. Stand fully tall — hips locked, shoulders back. Lower with control.
why: The conventional deadlift is the king of posterior chain development — glutes, hamstrings, spinal erectors, and traps all working together to lift maximal load from the floor. For hockey players, it builds the raw pulling and hip-hinge strength that underpins skating power, board battles, and spinal resilience. NHL strength coaches use deadlift strength (relative to bodyweight) as a primary indicator of an athlete's physical readiness.
transfer: Full-body strength king — builds power from the floor up. Three rep sets at 80-85%. Conventional is taxing — three working sets is plenty. Quality > volume.
cues: "Bar over laces" · "Big breath brace core" · "Push floor away" · "Hips and shoulders rise together"
mistakes: Bar drifting away from the body — drags the bar back in close. Treat it like a leg press. Jerking the bar off the floor — take the slack out first, then apply steady force. Rounding the lower back — set the brace before pulling. No exceptions. Hyperextending at the top — stand neutral, not leaned back.
progression: Progress: Deficit deadlift (stand on 2-inch plates) — increases ROM and starting position difficulty. | Regress: Trap bar deadlift — same hip hinge, more upright torso, less technical demand.

name: Hamstring Walkout
execution: Lie on your back, knees bent, feet flat on the floor. Drive hips up into a bridge position — same as a glute bridge. From the top, walk both feet forward — sliding the heels away from your body. Walk as far as you can while keeping the hips elevated and the back flat. Once at maximum extension, walk back in to the start. Keep the hips up the entire time — they must not sag.
why: The hamstring walkout eccentrically loads the hamstrings through their full length — from the hip to the knee — which is the exact injury mechanism of a hamstring strain (high-speed running or explosive skating stride at full extension). Eccentric hamstring strength is the primary protective factor against hamstring tears, and the walkout builds it without any equipment at all.
transfer: Eccentric hamstring control — major injury prevention for hockey sprinters. Three sets × 5 reps. Slow and controlled — the walk-out is where the hamstring loads, the walk-back is where the core works.
cues: "Walk heels out while in bridge" · "Maintain hip height" · "Walk back in"
mistakes: Hips dropping as feet walk out — the hamstrings must hold the hips up. If they drop, shorten the range. Too fast — slow and controlled eccentric loading is the entire point. Only doing the walk-out without the walk-back — the concentric return also matters. Skipping it because it seems too easy at short range — going to full extension is genuinely hard.
progression: Progress: Single-leg hamstring walkout — one foot elevated, walk out on a single leg. | Regress: Short-range walkout (feet only go out 15-20cm) until full-range hip-hold is achievable.

name: Leg Curl (Machine)
execution: Lie face-down on the leg curl machine. Pad sits just above the heels. Grip the handles for stability. Keep hips flat on the pad throughout. Curl both heels toward the glutes as far as possible. Squeeze the hamstrings hard at full contraction. Pause 1 second. Lower slowly — 3-4 seconds — to full extension. Do not let hips rise off the pad during the curl.
why: The leg curl isolates the hamstrings in knee flexion — the function that decelerates the leg at the end of each skating stride. While deadlifts and RDLs train the hamstrings in hip extension, the leg curl is the only exercise that specifically develops the knee flexion strength that protects the ACL under dynamic loading. NHL injury data consistently shows hamstring-to-quad ratio (ideally above 0.6) as a key ACL injury risk factor.
transfer: Isolates hamstrings — balances quad dominance common in hockey players. Pair leg curl with RDL on the same day for double hamstring stimulus. Insurance against the April pull.
cues: "Curl fully" · "Squeeze at peak contraction" · "Slow lowering phase"
mistakes: Hips lifting off the pad to complete the range — reduces hamstring isolation. Too fast on the way down — the 3-4 second eccentric is where injury prevention happens. Only doing bilateral — add single-leg curls to identify and correct imbalances.',. Going too heavy — proper form requires smooth full-range motion, not grinding.',.
progression: Progress: Nordic curl — the gold standard eccentric hamstring exercise.', | Regress: Hamstring walkout on the floor — same eccentric demand with no machine needed.',

name: Nordic Hamstring Curl
execution: Kneel on a pad, feet anchored under a bar, bench, or held by a partner. Arms crossed on chest or ready to catch you. Body perfectly upright — hips extended, torso in line with thighs. Slowly lower your body FORWARD toward the floor — resist the fall using the hamstrings. Lower as slowly as possible. When you can no longer resist, catch yourself with hands. Push back up with the hands and use the hamstrings to pull back to the upright start.
why: The Nordic curl is the most evidence-based hamstring injury prevention exercise in existence — multiple RCTs show it reduces hamstring strain risk by 51%. It eccentrically loads the hamstring from full knee extension through flexion, exactly the position of maximum strain during explosive skating. NFL, NHL, and soccer teams mandate Nordic curls after injury data became undeniable. Two sessions per week is enough for significant protection.
transfer: The single best exercise to prevent hamstring tears — critical for hockey players. If you can do 12 reps, you're elite. Most pros can do 6-8. Don't rush the standard.
cues: "Kneel" · "Partner holds ankles" · "Lower body as slow as possible" · "Push up with hands"
mistakes: Hips bending — the hips must stay extended. Hinge at the knee only. Dropping too fast — maximum eccentric resistance is the entire stimulus. Only doing the negative — the pull-back concentric also matters. Skipping it because it's hard — the difficulty is proportional to the protection it provides.
progression: Progress: Add a resistance band across the back for more eccentric load on the way down. | Regress: Hamstring walkout on the floor — same eccentric demand with fully bodyweight support.

name: Reverse Nordic Hold
execution: Kneel on a padded surface — folded towel, yoga mat, or carpet works. Knees hip-width, toes pointing back behind you (feet flat or pointed, your choice). Push your hips slightly forward and engage the glutes. Slowly lean backward — body stays in one straight line from knees to head. Stop where it gets hard — your eventual goal is hands able to touch the floor behind you, but start much shallower. HOLD. Tight glutes the whole hold. Return to upright under control.
why: The reverse Nordic is one of the very few exercises that loads the quads in their LENGTHENED position — the same angle the quad reaches at the back end of a hard deceleration or stop, where strains happen. Most quad training (squats, lunges, leg press) loads the muscle in a shortened or mid-range position, leaving the lengthened end of the strength curve untrained. That gap is exactly where injuries occur. A 20-30 second iso hold in the deepest reverse-Nordic position builds tissue tolerance precisely where it's needed for hockey: protecting against quad strains, building tendon stiffness around the kneecap, and adding the kind of bombproof anterior chain that lets a player decelerate from full speed on demand.
transfer: Loads the quads in the LENGTHENED position — the exact angle they fail at during hard decelerations. A rare quality you can't train any other way; protects against quad strains and patellar pain. Don't grind through pinching at the kneecap — that means you've gone too far. Find the position where it's hard but not sharp.
cues: "Kneel on a pad" · "Knees hip-width" · "Toes pointed back. Lean backward as far as you can control — hips push slightly forward" · "Body straight from knees to head. HOLD where it gets hard."
mistakes: Bending at the hips to fake range — defeats the exercise; body stays straight knees-to-head. Going too deep too fast — quad strains happen here; progress 5° per week max. Sharp pinching pain at the kneecap — back off immediately; that means you've gone past tolerance. Skipping the knee pad — bare knees on a hard floor end the set before the quads do.
progression: Progress: Reverse Nordic with arms overhead — adds anterior-chain demand and moment arm. Eventually full bottom range with hands on the floor behind you. | Regress: Shallow reverse Nordic — lean only 15-20° back, hands on thighs for support.

name: Romanian Deadlift (RDL)
execution: Hold a barbell or dumbbells in front of the thighs, arms straight. Stand tall — soft bend in the knees, this is NOT a locked-knee movement. Hinge at the hips: push them BACK while lowering the weight along the legs. Feel the hamstrings stretch as the weight descends to mid-shin. Keep the back flat — same neutral spine as a deadlift setup. Drive the hips forward to return to standing. Squeeze glutes at the top.
why: The Romanian deadlift (RDL) is the premier hamstring and glute strength builder — it trains the hip hinge under load through a large range of motion without the complexity of a conventional deadlift. For hockey players, strong hamstrings from RDLs directly reduce hamstring strain risk during explosive skating, improve stride extension, and build the posterior chain balance needed to offset the quad-dominant skating pattern.
transfer: Builds hamstring and glute strength — drives skating extension. Three seconds down, one second up. The eccentric is where the hamstring grows. Don't bounce.
cues: "Hip hinge" · "Soft knees" · "Bar close to legs" · "Feel hamstrings stretch" · "Drive hips forward"
mistakes: Bending the knees too much — turns it into a deadlift. Keep the slight knee bend consistent. Rounding the lower back — neutral spine throughout. Chest tall. Bar drifting away from the legs — keep it dragging along the shins and thighs. Not going low enough — aim for mid-shin before returning.
progression: Progress: Single-leg RDL — unilateral loading with massive balance and hip stability demand. | Regress: Dumbbell RDL — easier to keep the weight close to the body and control the range.

name: Russian Kettlebell Swing
execution: Stand with feet slightly wider than hip-width. Bell on the floor slightly in front. Hinge at the hips, grip the bell with both hands. Hike the bell back between the legs like a centre snapping a football. Drive the hips FORWARD explosively — stand up fast. The bell floats up. Let the bell float to chest height — it's the hip snap that drives it, not the arms. As the bell falls, hinge back immediately — load for the next rep.
why: The kettlebell swing is one of the most explosive posterior chain exercises available — it trains hip extension power at high velocity through a ballistic hip hinge. The pattern directly mirrors the skating push-off: hips load back, then snap forward with maximum force. Practically every strength coach working with hockey players lists the KB swing as a cornerstone exercise. It is also one of the safest high-velocity exercises for the lower back.
transfer: Hip-hinge ballistic — develops explosive hip extension without barbell load. Direct transfer to skating push-off. Cheap, simple, effective. Don't overthink it.
cues: "Hike between legs" · "Snap hips through hard" · "Swing to chest height (not overhead). Glutes and hams do all the work."
mistakes: Squatting instead of hinging — hips go BACK first, then snap forward. Not a squat. Pulling the bell with the arms — the arms are just ropes. Hips do the work. Bell going overhead — this is a swing, not a snatch. Shoulder height is enough. Lower back rounding at the bottom — maintain a flat back through the hinge.
progression: Progress: Single-arm kettlebell swing — adds rotational core demand and unilateral loading. | Regress: Romanian deadlift — teaches the hip hinge pattern before adding the ballistic element.',

name: Single-Leg Glute Bridge
execution: Lie on your back, one knee bent with foot flat, the other leg extended straight. Squeeze the glute of the bent-knee leg before moving. Drive the hips up through the planted foot — the straight leg stays in line with the body. Hold the top position 2-3 seconds. Feel the glute of the working leg fire. Lower slowly. Don't let the hip drop on the non-working side. Complete all reps one side, then switch.
why: The single-leg glute bridge isolates each glute independently, revealing and correcting the left-right strength imbalance that every hockey player has from years of dominant-side skating. A weak glute on the non-dominant side leads to compensatory lower-back loading and knee stress. Correcting this asymmetry is one of the highest-ROI injury prevention interventions available.
transfer: Unilateral glute strength — corrects side-to-side imbalances. If your hips tilt or rotate at the top, the glute med is weak. Bridge work is the cheapest fix.
cues: "One leg extended" · "Drive hip up with other leg" · "Squeeze glute at top"
mistakes: Hip dropping on the free leg side — this means the glute isn't fully engaged. Reset and squeeze harder. Lower back taking over instead of the glute — focus the contraction at the hip, not the spine. Equal reps both sides without noting which is weaker — track and give the weak side extra volume. Moving too fast — each rep needs the full 2-3 second hold at the top.
progression: Progress: Single-leg hip thrust (shoulders on bench, one leg extended) — loaded version. | Regress: Two-leg glute bridge — master the bilateral version before isolating.

name: Single-Leg Glute Bridge Hold
execution: Lie on your back, knees bent, one foot flat on the floor close to your butt. Extend the other leg straight in the air (or hold the knee bent at 90° if it's easier). Drive the planted heel hard into the floor and lift the hips to a straight line shoulder-to-knee. HOLD at the top. Squeeze the glute on the working side HARD — that's the whole stimulus. Ribs down, core tight, no arching at the lower back. Lower under control. Switch legs. That's one rep per leg.
why: Hockey is quad-dominant — every stride pushes through the front of the leg, and over a season the glutes/hamstrings get under-trained relative to their countering role. That imbalance is one of the top drivers of low-back pain and hamstring strains in skaters. The single-leg glute bridge hold isolates one glute at a time in a top-position isometric — no lower-back load, no equipment, maximum posterior-chain stimulus. Holding the top of a bridge for 30+ seconds builds the deep glute strength that translates to a harder stride push AND protects the lumbar spine across a long season.
transfer: Single-leg posterior-chain isometric. Counterbalances the quad-dominant demand of skating, protects the lower back, and stronger glutes mean a harder stride push. Feeling it more in the hamstring than the glute? Your foot's too far from your butt — pull it in a few inches.
cues: "Lie on your back" · "One foot flat on the floor close to your butt" · "Other leg extended in the air. Drive the planted heel down and lift to a straight line shoulder-to-knee. HOLD. Squeeze the glute hard. Switch legs."
mistakes: Feeling it in the hamstring instead of the glute — foot is too far from the butt; pull it in 2-3 inches. Over-arching the lower back to get higher — that's pelvic tilt, not glute drive; ribs stay down. Lifted leg sagging — keep it actively engaged so the working hip doesn't twist. Pushing through the toes — the heel is the driver; toes can even lift off the floor.
progression: Progress: Single-leg glute bridge hold with feet elevated on a bench — same hold, deeper hip extension range. | Regress: Two-leg glute bridge hold — earn 45-60s clean before going single-leg.

name: Single-Leg RDL
execution: Stand on one leg, soft bend in the knee. Hold a dumbbell in the opposite hand. Hinge at the hip — the torso lowers forward as the free leg rises behind. The free leg and torso should move together like a see-saw — hip as the pivot. Lower until the torso is roughly parallel to the floor and the hamstring is stretched. Drive the standing hip forward to return to upright — squeeze the glute. All reps one side before switching.
why: The single-leg Romanian deadlift is simultaneously a posterior chain strengthening exercise AND a balance and proprioception drill — making it one of the most efficient hockey exercises available. It trains the glute and hamstring of the standing leg under significant load while the hip must stabilise in all planes, directly replicating the balance demands of skating on one edge. It also reveals and corrects left-right hamstring strength imbalances.
transfer: Builds single-leg hamstring strength and balance — reduces injury risk. Three sets × 8 per leg, light dumbbell. Slow descent, drive up through the standing-leg glute.
cues: "Stand on one leg holding a DB or KB in the opposite hand. Hinge from the hip — opposite leg extends straight back as the torso tips forward" · "Back flat. Feel the standing-leg hamstring stretch. Drive the hip forward to stand up. Both sides equally."
mistakes: Hip rotating open — keep the hips square to the floor throughout. Free leg bent — keep it straight, in line with the torso. Looking down — neutral neck, eyes 2-3m ahead on the floor. Rushing to the advanced load before balance is established — bodyweight first.
progression: Progress: Double dumbbell single-leg RDL — heavier load with more balance challenge. | Regress: TRX-assisted single-leg RDL — light hand support allows the balance pattern to be learned.

name: Single-Leg RDL Hold
execution: Stand on one leg, other foot lifted just behind you. Hinge at the hip — chest drops forward, back leg lifts behind you in a straight line. Continue until torso is roughly parallel to the floor (or as deep as your hamstring tolerance allows). Back leg straight, toe pointed, hip square (don't let the back-leg hip rotate open). HOLD. Neutral spine — no rounding, no over-arching. Stand under control by driving the standing-leg heel down. Switch legs.
why: The single-leg RDL held at the bottom is the closest off-ice analogue to a fully-extended skating stride — back leg behind you, torso angled forward, force driving back into the ground. It's a hamstring isometric in the lengthened position, a glute strength drill, AND a balance/spinal-control test all in one rep. Building hamstring strength in this lengthened position is one of the most well-documented ways to reduce hamstring strains in any sport that involves sprinting or skating push-offs. For hockey, the bonus is the unilateral nature: single-leg work exposes the asymmetries every skater has and forces both sides to develop equally.
transfer: Hamstring iso plus balance plus spinal control all at once. The closest off-ice analogue to a fully-extended stride position — back leg driving force back into the surface. Twist open at the hip and the hold's lost. The whole exercise is in keeping the hips closed.
cues: "Stand on one leg. Hinge forward — chest drops" · "Back leg lifts behind you. Stop when your torso is roughly parallel to the floor. HOLD. Tight back leg" · "Neutral spine" · "Hips SQUARE. Switch legs."
mistakes: Back-leg hip rotating open — same fault as the hip airplane; hips stay SQUARE. Rounding the lower back — neutral spine; if you can't hold flat, you're hinging too deep for your current hamstring length. Standing knee locking out — keep a soft bend so the hamstring takes the load, not the joint. Catching with the back foot when balance fails — end the set; hold is over.
progression: Progress: Weighted single-leg RDL hold — dumbbell in the opposite-side hand (forces extra anti-rotation work). | Regress: Single-leg RDL hold with light hand support on a wall or rack — same hold, less balance demand.
muscles: Hamstrings, Glutes, Spinal erectors, Hip stabilizers

name: Sumo Deadlift
execution: Stance wider than shoulder-width, toes pointing out 30-45°. Bend down and grip the bar narrow — inside the legs. Hips are lower at the start than in conventional — more squat-like. Push knees out in line with toes. Chest tall, lats engaged. Drive the floor away — push the knees out as the bar rises. Stand fully — hips lock, shoulders back. Lower with control.
why: The sumo deadlift uses a wide stance and narrower grip — reducing lumbar flexion demand and shifting more load to the hip abductors and adductors than the conventional deadlift. For hockey players with groin or hip restrictions, the sumo stance is often more comfortable and still builds enormous posterior chain strength. The wide stance also closely mirrors the hip position in a max-effort skating stride.
transfer: Wide stance targets adductors — the inner thigh muscles critical for edge power. Triple extension at the top: hips, knees, ankles. Don't hyperextend the lower back — that's hips through, not back arch.
cues: "Wide stance" · "Toes out" · "Chest tall" · "Drive knees out" · "Pull bar up close"
mistakes: Knees caving inward — push them out aggressively throughout the lift. Bar drifting forward — keep it over the mid-foot. Hips rising faster than the chest — maintain the initial back angle off the floor. Stance too wide to control — find the width where you can push the knees out comfortably.
progression: Progress: Deficit sumo deadlift (stand on plates) — increases starting ROM demand. | Regress: Goblet squat — teaches the wide stance and knee-out mechanics before loading a bar.

name: Trap Bar Deadlift
execution: Load the trap bar. Step inside, feet hip-width, toes forward. Hinge at the hips and grab the handles with arms straight. Set the chest tall, lats engaged ('protect armpits'), shins close to vertical. Take a HUGE breath, brace the abs like you're about to take a punch. Drive feet through the floor — push the ground away. Bar travels straight up. Stand fully upright with hips locked. Don't hyperextend the lower back. Lower with control on the way down — eccentric matters.
why: The trap bar deadlift produces hip extension force equal to a conventional deadlift but with significantly less spinal load. This makes it the preferred max-strength tool for hockey players, where lower-back resilience matters as much as raw strength. The neutral handle position also lets you move heavier loads with cleaner mechanics — a strong predictor of skating sprint times.
transfer: Safer deadlift variation — excellent for developing overall power. Trap bar pulls are the closest weighted analog to a vertical jump. Heavy AND fast.
cues: "Stand centered" · "Neutral spine" · "Push through heels" · "Extend hips and knees simultaneously"
mistakes: Rounding the lower back — disqualifies the rep. Reset and use less weight. Hips shooting up first — turns it into a stiff-leg deadlift. Push KNEES away as you drive up. Hyperextending at the top — neutral spine, full glute squeeze, that's it. Skipping the eccentric (dropping the bar) — leaves 50% of the strength benefit on the table.
progression: Progress: Deficit trap bar deadlift (stand on 25mm plates) — extends ROM and challenges the bottom position. | Regress: Romanian deadlift first — less complex setup, better for learning the hip hinge before adding heavy load.

name: Cossack Squat Hold
execution: Stand in a wide stance, feet roughly 1.5× shoulder width, toes slightly turned out. Shift your weight onto one leg, dropping into a deep side squat. Opposite leg is straight, toes pointing up (heel may rest on floor). Working leg: heel stays planted, knee tracks over the toes. Torso stays tall — chest up, not collapsed forward. HOLD at the bottom. Stand under control. Switch sides. That's one rep per side.
why: The cossack squat hold places you in the deepest lateral position the human body trains — one leg deeply flexed, the other extended straight out to the side. It's an adductor isometric in the lengthened position (rare and valuable), a hip-mobility-under-load drill (rarer still), and a glute med/quad iso for the working side all at once. For hockey players, this directly trains the bottom of a crossover position — that moment when one skate is deeply loaded on an inside edge while the other is fully extended pushing off. The transfer to skating mechanics is immediate, AND the lengthened adductor iso is one of the only off-ice ways to keep groin tissue tolerant to the stretch loads of an aggressive change of direction.
transfer: Deep lateral-squat isometric — adductor lengthened-position hold plus hip mobility under load. Direct carryover to the deepest part of a crossover and the recovery phase after a hard stride. Tight ankles or hips will limit depth — go as deep as you can keep the heel down. Don't cheat onto the toe.
cues: "Wide stance" · "Toes slightly out. Shift weight onto one leg" · "Drop into a deep side squat — opposite leg straight" · "Toes up. HOLD at the bottom. Tight torso" · "Heel down. Switch legs."
mistakes: Working heel coming off the floor — limits depth and ruins the position; if you can't keep it down, you're too deep. Torso collapsing forward — defeats the iso for the adductors of the straight leg; chest stays up. Knee caving inward on the working side — push it out toward the toes actively. Forcing depth you don't have — ankle and hip mobility limit this exercise; respect the limit and progress over weeks.
progression: Progress: Weighted cossack hold (goblet a kettlebell at the chest). Or full-depth cossack with butt-to-heel position. | Regress: Supported cossack hold — light hand on a pole/wall for balance. Or shallower depth as you build mobility.

name: Crossover Lunge (DBs)
execution: Stand with feet hip-width. Hands on hips or holding light dumbbells. Step the right foot diagonally ACROSS and BEHIND the left leg — like a curtsy. Lower the rear (right) knee toward the floor. Keep the front (left) knee tracking over the toes — don't let it cave in. Front foot stays flat on the floor throughout. Drive back up through the front heel to return to standing. Alternate sides or complete all reps one side first.
why: The crossover lunge trains the hip abductors and adductors in the exact diagonal loading pattern of a skating crossover. By stepping across and behind the body, you create a rotational hip demand that bilateral lunges cannot replicate. This is why it transfers so directly to crossover speed and edge-to-edge transitions, particularly in tight turns.
transfer: Trains hip abductors and rotators — key for crossover skating power. Three sets × 8 per leg. Slow, controlled — the depth of the lunge is where the glute med earns its money.
cues: "Step across body at diagonal" · "Lower into lunge" · "Drive back to start"
mistakes: Front knee caving inward — drive it out over the little toe. Torso collapsing forward — stay upright, chest proud. Not crossing far enough behind — a short step reduces the hip abductor demand. Losing balance — slow down and master the bodyweight version first.
progression: Progress: Add a lateral band resistance or hold a weighted plate overhead for increased challenge. | Regress: Reverse lunge — same pattern without the crossover, easier to balance.

name: Dumbbell Step-Up
execution: Face a box or bench (30-50cm). Place one foot fully on top. Drive through the box foot — extend hip and knee to stand fully on top. Bring the trailing foot up. Stand tall — full hip extension at the top. Step back down with control. The driving leg stays on the box. Complete all reps one side before switching. Add dumbbells at sides as bodyweight becomes easy.
why: The step-up is the foundational single-leg vertical strength exercise — building the glute, quad, and hip control needed for powerful skating push-offs. Because one leg is working while the other only supports, it identifies and corrects bilateral strength deficits that compound over a career of dominant-side skating. A basic but essential movement that should be in every hockey player's program at some point.
transfer: Single-leg strength in the exact pattern of skating stride. Three sets × 8 per leg, controlled tempo. Heavy enough that the last rep is honest.
cues: "Full foot on box" · "Drive through heel" · "Stand tall at top" · "Lower with control"
mistakes: Pushing off the floor foot — all drive from the box leg only. Knee caving inward — push it out over the toes. Not reaching full hip extension at the top — stand TALL on each rep. Box too low — at or above knee height for real demand.
progression: Progress: Lateral step-up then crossover step-up — progress through the variations. | Regress: Low step (20cm) step-up — build confidence and stability before raising the height.

name: Lateral Step-Up
execution: Stand beside a box (30-50cm), side-on. Place the near foot fully on the top of the box. Drive through the box foot — extend hip and knee — to stand on top. Bring the trailing foot up to meet the top foot. Stand tall. Step back down with control. The driving leg stays on the box. Complete all reps one side before switching.',.
why: The lateral step-up trains the glute med and hip abductors through a vertical range in a single-leg lateral loading pattern — the exact demand of the support phase during a skating stride. Standing to the side of the box and stepping up laterally creates a hip abductor drive that bilateral or forward step-ups cannot replicate. It is a fundamental building block in all hockey strength programs.
transfer: Trains lateral hip strength — mirrors the side push of skating. Three sets × 8 per leg, controlled. If you push off the down-foot, you cheated. Front foot only.
cues: "Step up sideways onto box" · "Drive through lateral leg" · "Stand tall" · "Lower slowly"
mistakes: Pushing off the floor foot — all power from the box leg. Knee caving inward — drive it outward over the little toe.',. Box too low — knee height or above for real demand. No pause at the top — stand fully upright on each rep.',.
progression: Progress: Weighted lateral step-up with dumbbells, then progress to a lateral step-up with knee drive at the top.', | Regress: Step-up to a lower surface (20cm) until single-leg stability is established.',

name: Paused Split Squat (Isometric)
execution: Take a long split-squat stance — front foot flat, back foot on its toe. Lower straight down — back knee descends until 1 inch from the floor. HOLD. Front shin roughly vertical, back leg extended. Tight glutes both sides. Core braced. Hips square (don't twist). Hold until form breaks. Stand. Switch legs. That's one rep per leg.
why: The paused split squat is a unilateral isometric — single-leg loading held in the deepest position. It directly trains the position of a defensive crouch, a goalie's lateral push-off, or absorbing contact when you're caught mid-stride on one leg. Unilateral isometrics expose left-right imbalances ruthlessly (you can't compensate by leaning) — making this one of the best diagnostic AND development tools for hockey-specific lower-body strength.
transfer: Single-leg isometric hold at the bottom of a split squat — the exact pattern of holding a defensive crouch or absorbing contact one-legged. Triphasic isometric phase, unilateral. Useful diagnostic: if one leg shakes 10 seconds earlier than the other, that's the priority side.
cues: "Take a split-squat stance. Lower until back knee hovers 1 inch from floor. HOLD there. Front knee tracks over toes. Tight glutes. Switch legs."
mistakes: Front knee caving inward — same ACL-risk pattern; track it over the second toe. Hips twisting toward the back leg — re-square them; this is the silent test of hip stability. Holding too shallow (back knee 6+ inches off the floor) — the deep position is the whole point. Bouncing in and out — kills the isometric stimulus. Hold STILL.
progression: Progress: Weighted pause split squat — hold dumbbells at sides or a barbell on the back. | Regress: Pause split squat with hand support (light touch on a bench or chair) — same hold, less balance demand.
muscles: Quadriceps, Glutes, Hip stabilizers, Isometric strength

name: Poliquin Step-Up (DBs)
execution: Stand facing a step (15-20cm high) with one foot on the step, heel at the edge. The other foot hangs off the back — this is the non-working leg. Lower the hanging heel toward the floor by bending the step knee. Descend until the hanging heel barely touches the floor. Drive back up through the step heel to standing. All reps one leg before switching. Feel it in the inner quad.
why: The Poliquin step-up (also called the Bulgarian step-up) specifically targets the VMO (vastus medialis oblique) — the teardrop quad muscle that stabilises the knee cap during the skating knee-bend. Charles Poliquin developed it for hockey players specifically. Weak VMO is directly linked to patellar tracking issues and ACL injury. This exercise addresses the VMO in isolation better than any other movement.
transfer: Directly targets the VMO — prevents knee injuries common in hockey. Three sets × 8 per leg with dumbbells. Slow tempo, full ROM, both legs balanced.
cues: "Low box" · "Step up on toes" · "Drive through heel" · "Feel inner quad contract"
mistakes: Step too high — reduces VMO isolation. 15-20cm is the optimal height. Pushing off the hanging foot — all work from the step leg. Not going low enough — the descent must be sufficient to fully load the VMO. Going too fast — slow, controlled movement maximises VMO activation.
progression: Progress: Add dumbbells or a weight vest as bodyweight becomes easy. | Regress: Terminal knee extension (TKE) with band — even more isolated VMO activation.

name: Single-Leg Press
execution: Set up as a standard leg press but place only one foot on the platform. The working foot is centred — mid-height on the platform. Control the descent — 2-3 seconds down to 90° knee bend. Drive through the full foot to press back up. Stop just short of full lock-out. Complete all reps on one leg before switching. Note the load difference between legs — work to close the gap.
why: The single-leg press isolates each leg independently on the leg press machine, correcting the strength imbalances that develop from years of dominant-side skating mechanics. Research consistently shows hockey players have 10-20% strength differences between legs — a deficit directly linked to asymmetrical injury risk and power leakage in the skating stride. Equal bilateral leg press strength correlates with more symmetrical skating mechanics.
transfer: Corrects leg imbalances — most hockey players have a stronger push leg. Pair with single-leg RDL for full unilateral lower-body day. Quad + hamstring, both sides, no compensation.
cues: "One foot centered" · "Lower to 90°" · "Press through heel" · "Full range of motion"
mistakes: Knee caving inward during the press — drive it outward over the toes. Too much load — single-leg is roughly 60-65% of your bilateral leg press max. Not noting the imbalance — if you never measure it, you never fix it. Locking out the knee explosively — controlled extension only.
progression: Progress: Progress toward equal loading on both legs — the goal is bilateral symmetry. | Regress: Leg press with one foot slightly lighter on the platform before going fully single-leg.

name: Single-Leg Wall Sit
execution: Stand with your back flat against a wall, feet about 50 cm out. Slide down until both thighs are parallel to the floor. Brace your core, then lift one foot 1-2 inches off the floor. All the load is now on the planted leg. Keep the thigh parallel — don't let it rise. HOLD. Hips stay level (no dropping toward the lifted side). Stand, recover briefly, repeat on the other leg. That's one rep per leg.
why: A standard wall sit is a brutal quad isometric, but it lets the stronger side compensate — most skaters have a noticeable left/right asymmetry from years of pushing off one leg harder than the other, and a bilateral wall sit hides that. Single-leg wall sit forces each leg to hold the entire load on its own, exposing the asymmetry AND building the weak side directly. The 90° quad isometric in this position is the exact muscle quality of holding a deep skating stance on a single edge — pure off-ice transfer to crossover support and tight-turn outside-leg loading.
transfer: Unilateral wall-sit progression that exposes the left/right asymmetry every skater develops. Single-leg isometric quad endurance — the muscle quality of holding a deep stance on one edge. If one side is 10+ seconds weaker, that's your priority leg. Train the weak side first while you're freshest.
cues: "Wall sit at parallel — thighs flat" · "Knees at 90°. Lift one foot off the floor. Bottom leg holds everything. No hip drop" · "No twisting. HOLD. Switch legs."
mistakes: Hips dropping toward the lifted side — kills the unilateral stimulus; squeeze the planted glute to hold them level. Letting the planted thigh rise above parallel as it gets hard — slide back down or end the set. Resting the lifted foot on the planted shin — that's a sneaky cheat; keep it hovering. Going single-leg before the bilateral version is solid — earn a 90s bilateral wall sit first.
progression: Progress: Single-leg wall sit holding a kettlebell at the chest — same hold, much more load. | Regress: Bilateral wall sit — earn 60-90s solid before going single-leg.

name: Skater Squat
execution: Stand on one leg. The other leg extends behind — NOT touching the floor. Hold a small counterweight (2-5kg plate) at chest height for balance. Lower by bending the standing knee and hinging slightly at the hip. The rear leg swings back for counterbalance. Descend until the rear knee nearly touches the floor. Drive through the heel to stand. Complete all reps then switch.
why: The skater squat (rear-foot-free single-leg squat) is arguably the most demanding unilateral lower-body exercise — it requires simultaneous strength, balance, and hip mobility on a single leg with no rear foot assistance. For hockey players it builds the skating-specific single-leg strength and proprioception that transfers directly to powerful, stable stride mechanics. Mastering this correlates strongly with elite single-leg skating power output.
transfer: Single-leg squat that perfectly mimics the skating position. Three sets × 5 per leg. Difficult enough that 5 honest reps is plenty.
cues: "Balance on one leg" · "Swing arms forward as you lower" · "Tap knee to pad" · "Drive up"
mistakes: Falling forward — the counterweight at the chest helps. If still falling, reduce depth. Rear foot touching the floor for support — it must stay elevated. Knee caving inward — drive it out over the toes. Only going half depth — full range builds full-range strength.
progression: Progress: Hold heavier counterweight or add dumbbells at sides as balance and strength improve. | Regress: Bulgarian split squat — rear foot supported, building the pattern before going unsupported.

name: Skater Squat Bottom Hold
execution: Stand on one leg, other leg bent slightly behind you (knee toward the floor). Reach both arms forward as a counterweight. Squat down on the standing leg — the back knee descends toward (but doesn't touch) the floor. HOLD at the bottom: back knee 1-3 inches off the floor, front shin vertical or slightly forward. Tight glute, knee tracks over toes, torso tall (don't dive forward). Stand under control. Switch legs. That's one rep per leg.
why: The skater squat held at the bottom is the closest off-ice match to the loaded edge position of a tight turn or crossover. Both knees and hips sit at the angles a skater's joints actually live in during the hardest skating positions — not the upright 90° of a normal squat, but the deeper, more diagonal angle where the outside leg loads through an edge. Holding this position builds knee stability and quad/glute strength in the SPECIFIC range hockey demands, in a position where most off-ice training never goes. That's what makes it elite-level transfer for skating.
transfer: Deep single-leg squat held at the bottom — the exact knee/hip angle of tight turns and crossover edge work. Builds stability in the position skaters actually fail in. If the front knee dives inward, regress to bench-supported. Don't grind a bad position to add seconds.
cues: "Single-leg squat down — back knee hovers just above the floor" · "Arms forward as a counterweight. HOLD. Tight glute" · "Front shin vertical" · "Knee tracks the toes. Switch legs."
mistakes: Front knee diving inward as it gets hard — regress immediately; that's the ACL injury pattern. Crashing the back knee into the floor — defeats the hold; control the descent and hover. Diving the torso forward to balance — hips/knees stay deep, but chest stays up. Going single-leg before unilateral split squats are clean — build the base first.
progression: Progress: Weighted skater squat hold — goblet-hold a dumbbell or kettlebell at the chest. | Regress: Bench-supported skater squat hold — light hand on a chair/bench for balance; full hold remains.
muscles: Quadriceps, Glutes, Hip stabilizers, Knee stability

name: Band External Rotation
execution: Anchor a band at elbow height. Stand sideways to the anchor. Grip the band with the far hand. Tuck the elbow firmly against your side at 90°. Starting position: hand pointing toward the anchor (internally rotated). Rotate the hand AWAY from the anchor — externally rotating at the shoulder. Hold the fully-rotated position 2 seconds. Squeeze the back of the shoulder. Return slowly to start — 3 seconds. Elbow stays pinned to the side throughout.
why: External rotation weakness is the most common shoulder dysfunction in hockey players — years of internal rotation (stick handling, shooting, forward skating posture) create a dramatic imbalance. Weak external rotators are the primary cause of rotator cuff injuries and shoulder impingement. Two sets of band external rotation daily is the cheapest injury insurance a hockey player can buy.
transfer: Rotator cuff prehab — prevents the shoulder injuries common from repeated shooting. External rotation work is non-negotiable for any throwing or pressing athlete. Hockey players push and stick-check — same demand.
cues: "Elbow at 90°" · "Rotate arm out" · "Pause at end range" · "Return with control"
mistakes: Elbow drifting away from the side — it must stay pinned. Use a towel under the arm if needed. Using momentum or a fast snap — slow and controlled only. Band too heavy — range of motion suffers. Use a light band with full ROM. Only doing it when the shoulder hurts — daily prevention is the entire point.
progression: Progress: Side-lying dumbbell external rotation — heavier load, same movement. | Regress: Doorway stretch and isometric external rotation (push hand against a wall) before banding.

name: Barbell Bench Press
execution: Lie on the bench, eyes directly under the bar. Feet flat on floor. Grip slightly wider than shoulders. Wrists straight, NOT bent back. Set the upper back: pinch shoulder blades together and press them DOWN into the bench. Unrack with arms straight. Bring the bar over your sternum. Lower under control — about 2 seconds — to lower chest (nipple line). Bar touches lightly. Press up and slightly back, finishing over the shoulders. Lock out without flaring elbows. Keep the upper back tight for the entire set. Foot drive helps.
why: The bench press develops upper-body pressing strength — vital for protecting yourself in board contact, fending off defenders, and shot power transfer. NHL combine: top prospects bench 1.0-1.2× bodyweight. Hockey players need a balanced press-to-pull ratio (1:1) to avoid the chronic shoulder issues common with pressing-heavy programs.
transfer: Raw upper body pressing strength for checking and battle play. Three sets × 5-6 reps heavy on strength days. Five-rep sets are the sweet spot for hockey-specific pressing strength.
cues: "Arch back" · "Feet flat" · "Lower bar to lower chest" · "Drive up and slightly back"
mistakes: Flaring elbows 90° — shreds the shoulders. Keep elbows ~45-60° from torso. Bouncing the bar off the chest — converts a strength rep into a momentum-fueled cheat. Lifting glutes off the bench — disqualifies the rep in any context that matters. Bar drifting toward the throat — should stay over the chest at the bottom.
progression: Progress: Pause bench (1-2 sec on chest) builds bottom-end strength — direct transfer to checking off the boards. | Regress: Dumbbell bench press first — easier on shoulders, builds pattern with more freedom of movement.

name: Dead Hang
execution: Jump up and grip the pull-up bar slightly wider than shoulder-width. Let your body hang completely — arms straight, feet off the floor. Allow the shoulders to shrug up slightly (passive hang) — feel the spine decompress. Relax the entire body. Breathe steadily. Hold for the time prescribed on the workout card. Build up over weeks. If grip fails early, use chalk or straps to extend the set.
why: The dead hang decompresses the entire spinal column, counteracting the compressive forces of skating, lifting, and checking. It also builds grip strength and shoulder mobility — hanging from a bar with full shoulder elevation restores the overhead range chronically restricted by hockey posture. NHL medical staff recommend 60-second dead hangs daily as shoulder health maintenance for all positions.
transfer: Builds the grip and shoulder endurance needed before pull-ups become possible — also decompresses the spine. If you can dead-hang 60 seconds at bodyweight, you've earned grip work. If you can't, that's the homework.
cues: "Pronated grip" · "Arms fully extended" · "Shoulders engaged (not shrugged up to ears)" · "Brace core" · "Breathe"
mistakes: Actively pulling the shoulders down — the passive hang (shoulders elevated) decompresses the spine more effectively. Not doing it long enough — under 30 seconds provides minimal benefit. Swinging — stay still and control the hang. Skipping it because it's 'just hanging' — spinal decompression is serious recovery work.
progression: Progress: Single-arm dead hang — massively increases grip and shoulder demand. | Regress: Assisted hang (feet lightly touching the floor) — reduce load while building shoulder comfort.

name: Dumbbell Shoulder Press
execution: Sit on a bench with back support, or stand with feet shoulder-width. Hold dumbbells at shoulder height, elbows at about 75° angle (not flared straight out). Press the dumbbells up and slightly toward each other at the top. Fully lock out at the top — arms straight, biceps near the ears. Lower under control — 2-3 seconds down — back to the starting shoulder position. Keep the core braced — don't arch the lower back to push the weight.
why: Overhead pressing strength protects the shoulder joint during checks and physical play by strengthening the rotator cuff stabilizers under load. The dumbbell version is preferred over barbell for hockey players because independent arm movement allows natural shoulder tracking — reducing the impingement risk associated with fixed-bar overhead pressing on internally-rotated hockey shoulders.
transfer: Unilateral shoulder strength — corrects left/right imbalances from stick use. Pair with face pulls or band pull-aparts. Press shouldn't outweigh pull. 2:1 push-pull rule, always.
cues: "DBs at ear height or KBs in the rack position (handles at shoulder" · "Forearms vertical" · "Knuckles up). Press straight overhead" · "Control the descent."
mistakes: Flaring elbows to 90° — shoulder impingement risk. Bring elbows slightly forward. Arching the lower back aggressively — if this happens the weight is too heavy. Not reaching full lockout — you're leaving overhead mobility and shoulder health on the table. Rushing the eccentric — the lowering phase builds shoulder stability.
progression: Progress: Standing single-arm dumbbell press — adds massive core anti-lateral flexion demand. | Regress: Seated machine shoulder press — guided path reduces stabilization demand for beginners.

name: Incline Push-Up
execution: Place both hands on a bench, wall, or bar at chest height. The higher the surface, the easier. Walk feet back until the body forms a straight line — ankles to shoulders. Brace the core hard — no sagging hips. Lower the chest toward the surface, elbows at 45° from the torso. Touch the surface with the chest. Press back to full arm extension. Keep the body rigid throughout — don't let the hips pike or sag.
why: The incline push-up trains upper-body pressing strength with less absolute load than a standard push-up — making it the entry point for players who cannot yet perform quality flat push-ups. The incline shifts the load more toward the upper chest and shoulders. Despite being a beginner tool it is also used by advanced athletes for high-rep shoulder health work and pre-game activation.
transfer: Beginner pressing variation — builds shoulder stability and chest strength. Three sets × 12-15. Use this as your push-up grease-the-groove drill. Frequency beats intensity for bodyweight strength.
cues: "Hands on bench" · "Body plank" · "Lower chest toward bench" · "Full extension"
mistakes: Hips sagging — maintain a straight body line from ankles to shoulders. Elbows flaring to 90° — keep them at 45° to protect the shoulder. Head dropping forward — neutral neck, eyes looking slightly ahead of the hands. Short range of motion — chest must touch the surface and arms must fully extend.
progression: Progress: Standard push-up — reduce the incline progressively until you reach floor level. | Regress: Wall push-up — highest incline, minimal load. Entry point for complete beginners.

name: Overhead Press
execution: Hold a barbell or dumbbells at shoulder height, elbows slightly in front of the bar. Feet shoulder-width. Core braced hard — do NOT arch the lower back. Press the bar straight up — head moves slightly back to clear the bar path. Once the bar passes the forehead, head moves back under and bar travels in a straight line. Lock out fully at the top — biceps near the ears. Lower under control — 2-3 seconds — back to shoulders.
why: The overhead press builds the shoulder, upper trap, and tricep strength required for physical dominance in the corners and along the boards. For hockey players it also trains the core anti-extension under a vertically-loaded spine — the same bracing pattern needed during contact. Pressing strength overhead directly correlates with the ability to win puck battles when both players are fighting with their arms elevated.
transfer: Builds shoulder stability and overhead strength — important for physical play. Heavy overhead press = a healthy shoulder ten years from now. Skip it at your peril.
cues: "Bar at clavicle" · "Press overhead to lockout" · "Squeeze glutes to protect spine"
mistakes: Excessive lower back arch — if the back arches severely, the weight is too heavy. Bar path drifting forward — bar should travel in a straight vertical line. Not locking out at the top — full overhead range is what keeps shoulders healthy. Flaring elbows wide at the bottom — keep them slightly forward of the bar.
progression: Progress: Single-arm dumbbell press standing — adds massive core anti-lateral flexion demand. | Regress: Seated dumbbell press — back support reduces core demand for beginners.

name: Plate Pinch
execution: Hold two 10kg (or two 5kg) plates together with one hand — smooth sides facing out. Pinch the top edge with the fingers on one side and thumb on the other. Hold at your side — do not rest it on your leg. Hold as long as possible. Time it. Switch hands. Rest 90s between attempts. Build hold time progressively each week.
why: Plate pinching (gripping weight plates between the fingers and thumb) develops the finger flexor strength and pinch grip that directly translates to stick handling under defensive pressure. When a defender cross-checks your hands or you're fighting for a loose puck, pinch grip is what keeps the stick in your hands. Many elite forwards specifically credit grip training for improving their puck-protection ability.
transfer: Pinch grip strength = stick control + faceoff wins + holding the lane. Direct transfer to gameplay. Pair with farmer carries + wrist roller. Crush grip + carry grip + pinch grip = bulletproof hands.
cues: "Pinch 2 plates together (smooth side out). Hold for time. No straps. Squeeze hard the entire hold."
mistakes: Using the palm — pinch grip only. The palm should barely touch the plate. Resting the plate on the thigh — defeats the purpose. Arm hanging straight. Too heavy too soon — build the connective tissue gradually. Skipping the non-dominant hand — both hands equally important.
progression: Progress: Heavier plates or three-plate pinch — progressively more challenging. | Regress: Towel hang from a pull-up bar — grip strength with a different texture demand.

name: Push-Up Challenge (60s)
execution: Set a 60-second timer. Get into perfect push-up position. Begin. Pace yourself — go hard but not so hard you blow up in 15 seconds. Every rep must be full ROM: chest to floor, full lockout at top. When form breaks, REST for 2-3 seconds, then continue. Form is non-negotiable. When the timer hits zero, count only the perfect reps. Write it down. That's your baseline.
why: Max-rep push-ups in a fixed time window is a classic relative-strength benchmark — it measures how much pressing capacity you can express against your own bodyweight. Hockey demands both strength AND strength endurance: you need to win a battle in the first minute, but you also need to win one in the third period of OT. Tracking this number weekly is one of the simplest, most honest measures of whether your off-ice work is paying off.
